result:
There's a small magic trick your brain plays after you learn something new. You encounter an unfamiliar word—say, "petrichor," the smell of rain on dry earth—and within days it appears everywhere: in a novel, a podcast, a stranger's conversation at the bus stop. The word was always there, of course. You were simply blind to it, the way you're blind to your own nose until someone mentions it.

This is the frequency illusion, and I find it quietly wonderful. It means the world hasn't changed; your attention has. Learning isn't just adding new furniture to the mind—it's installing new windows. Suddenly light comes in from directions you didn't know existed.

I think about this whenever I pick up some fragment of knowledge. A little botany, and a walk becomes a crowd of named neighbors. A little music theory, and songs reveal their skeletons. A little history, and every street corner has a backstory. The world doesn't grow more interesting; we grow more capable of noticing its interest.

Maybe that's the best argument for curiosity: it's not about accumulating facts. It's about increasing the surface area of your attention, so more of reality can catch on you. Every new thing learned is a hook the world can snag on. And the more hooks you carry, the more texture everything has—a walk through the park becomes a feast instead of wallpaper.

The universe, it turns out, was always whispering. You just needed the vocabulary to hear it.
